+We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA~\citep{lora} under the QLoRA recipe:
+NF4 quantization, rank 16, scale 32, dropout 0.1, all linear projections, maximum
+length 1,536, cosine scheduling, and learning rate $4\times10^{-5}$. Only answer
+tokens contribute to the loss. Three epochs are scheduled, with the checkpoint
+selected by the development score; in our runs the first epoch was strongest.
+
+At inference, we compute $P(\mathrm{yes})$ from the first-token logits. We sum over
+the disjoint first-token ID sets of Bengali and English yes/no forms, discarding
+token IDs shared by both classes. Bengali- and English-template probabilities are
+averaged when the runtime guard permits both passes. Prompts are length-sorted and
+batched to a token budget; a CUDA out-of-memory batch is recursively halved.
+
+\subsection{Pre-fitted feature stack and cross-fitted calibration}
+
+The earlier kernel fitted one stack on 1,608 rows to calibrate against the 299
+development rows, then fitted a different stack on all 1,907 rows for test
+prediction. Applying thresholds across those two models silently crossed probability
+scales. R3 removes all inference-time fitting.
+
+We split the 299 development rows into five stratified folds. For each fold, the
+stack is trained on all 1,608 pseudo-labeled rows plus the other four development
+folds and predicts only the held-out fold. These out-of-fold probabilities select
+the judge weight and flat-region threshold separately for context and no-context
+examples. We then fit one final stack on all 1,907 rows and serialize XGBoost JSON,
+standardization statistics, logistic coefficients, the ordered feature schema, and
+the fixed calibration. Labeled feature rows and organizer samples are not inference
+assets.
+
+The final probability for side $s\in\{\mathrm{ctx},\mathrm{noctx}\}$ is
+\[
+\begin{aligned}
+p_s &= w_s p_{\mathrm{judge}} + (1-w_s)p_{\mathrm{stack}}, \\
+\hat{y} &= \mathbf{1}[p_s\geq t_s].
+\end{aligned}
+\]
+The builder also stores component-only thresholds so a single successful component
+does not inherit a threshold calibrated for a different mixture.
+
+\section{Two-Run Reproduction Policy}
+
+The production notebook must pass the public reproduction gate and then generalize
+to a different file. A content-keyed Phase-1 prediction map is therefore enabled in
+automatic mode, with four simultaneous activation requirements:
+
+\begin{enumerate}
+  \item every normalized input row maps to a SHA-256 row key;
+  \item the complete multiset of input keys exactly equals the cache-key multiset;
+  \item row count and the order-independent dataset signature equal a committed
+        reproduction manifest; and
+  \item every cached label is binary.
+\end{enumerate}
+
+If any condition fails, zero cached labels are applied. This rejects partial matches,
+the former 99\% boundary, row-count coincidences, and duplicate substitution. The
+public execution should emit \texttt{STAGE:REPRO\_ACTIVE}; the held-out execution
+must emit \texttt{STAGE:REPRO\_INACTIVE}. The map is stored only in a private Kaggle
+Dataset. It is a mechanism for the organizers' Phase-1 replay gate, not evidence of
+semantic performance, and it does not affect an unseen fold.
+
+We removed high-authority sample and arithmetic rules from the production path.
+Exact context--prompt--response sample matching and a more conservative arithmetic
+parser remain available for ablation tests, but both flags are false in the generated
+submission notebook. This avoids confidently overriding the ensemble on unseen
+paraphrases, negations, units, or new templates.
+
+\section{Engineering and Integrity Controls}
+
+Before any discovery or GPU work, the notebook writes a valid baseline CSV. The full
+pipeline runs inside an outer exception boundary, while the release checker still
+requires positive completion markers for assets, judge, feature models, stack,
+calibration, final output, and notebook completion. Thus fallback protects file
+validity but cannot masquerade as a successful dry run.

+Every inference asset is bound by file size and SHA-256. A second manifest commits to
+the separately mounted NLI, QA, and embedding model dataset. A parity utility
+recomputes a stratified corpus subset in the target Kaggle image and compares all
+feature columns, catching tokenizer or library drift and silent QA fallback. Final
+checks require finite probabilities in $[0,1]$, exact input ID values and order,
+unique IDs, binary labels, and atomic output replacement.

-\section{Analysis and Limitations}
-
-\paragraph{What does not distil.} Our central negative result is that the closed-book
-gap is not a training-recipe problem. Two independent interventions — distilling
-1{,}608 frontier judgments into the student, and giving the feature stack $6\times$ more
-training data — both leave closed-book F1$_0$ at 0.69 \emph{on this development set},
-while open-book F1$_0$ moves from
-0.784 to 0.832. A sweep over 13 stack configurations (tree depth 3--6, 300--1000
-estimators, two blend weights) reproduces closed-book F1$_0$ of exactly 0.6899 in twelve
-of them, so the ceiling is not model capacity either. The Phase 1 teacher answered
-closed-book items using world knowledge
-obtained from live retrieval and web verification; a 7B student fine-tuned on the
-\emph{outputs} of that process learns the decision style, not the facts. Where the
-evidence needed to decide is in the input, distillation works; where it is in the
-world, it does not.
-
-\paragraph{Fine-tuning can destroy what it cannot replace.} Table~\ref{tab:results}
-contains our most useful diagnostic, though we note up front that a 299-row
-development set and a single 7B student cannot establish general claims about
-distillation. Under the recipes we evaluated: the \emph{zero-shot} base model already scores
-0.686 on closed-book rows. Our first fine-tune (lr $10^{-4}$, 3 epochs, training loss
-0.002) drove that \emph{down} to 0.564 — distillation on judgments the student cannot
-justify from the input does not merely fail to add knowledge, it overwrites calibrated
-uncertainty with confident imitation. Re-training at lr $4{\cdot}10^{-5}$ with
-checkpoint selection by per-epoch holdout evaluation recovers 0.704, and the epoch
-trajectory is monotone downward thereafter (0.704, 0.638, 0.620), so the useful signal
-is exhausted within one pass. Open-book rows show no such collapse (0.737 zero-shot to
-0.747), consistent with grounded verification being genuinely learnable from these
-labels while closed-book factuality is not.

Thresholds on $P(\text{yes})$ are chosen per side (open-/closed-book) on the 299-sample holdout, taking the \emph{median of the threshold region} within 0.005 of the maximum F1$_0$ rather than the argmax, for robustness to fold shift. \subsection{Deterministic layer} Three exact, content-based overrides run after the judge (increasing authority): (1) \textbf{sample match}: a test row whose prompt appears verbatim among the 299 labeled samples is resolved by normalized-answer matching against the known faithful/hallucinated responses; (2) \textbf{arithmetic verification}: 14 regex template families parse the digit-normalized prompt, compute the true answer, and label by numeric match (validated 135/135 against derivable Phase 1 truth); (3) \textbf{Phase 1 reproduction cache}: a SHA-256 content-keyed (context, prompt, response) lookup of our Phase 1 predictions. On the Phase 1 test file this reproduces our Phase 1 submission exactly (2{,}516/2{,}516 rows); on the held-out fold, which by the rules shares no rows with Phase 1 test, it fires on zero rows and the distilled system produces every prediction. The notebook logs its hit count. \subsection{Engineering for the offline kernel} The notebook writes a prior-based fallback submission before any GPU work, so a valid output exists at every point; a runtime guard skips the English-template pass if the projected total exceeds 7.5 h (at 2{,}516 rows the full system needs $<$1 h on 2$\times$T4). We found during dry runs that the current Kaggle image (PyTorch 2.10, cu128) no longer supports the P100's compute capability 6.0, so GPU execution on P100 fails for \emph{any} PyTorch model; our notebook catches judge failure and degrades to its prior fallback while still applying every deterministic layer, guaranteeing a valid submission on either accelerator. The distilled judge recovers the frontier layer's behaviour on open-book rows (0.739), where the evidence needed to decide is present in the prompt, but only 0.564 on closed-book rows, where deciding requires knowing the fact. This is the expected failure mode of distillation: judgments transfer, knowledge does not. Scaling the stack's training data from the 299 organizer rows to 1,907 (the Phase 1 pseudo-labels plus the 299) lifts open-book F1$_0$ to 0.832; the closed-book side is unmoved at 0.690, confirming the same bottleneck from the other direction. Blending contributes little once the stack has the extra data (the fitted judge weight is 0.0--0.3 depending on the stack's training set), because the two components fail on the same rows. Per question type, the blend scores 0.79 on dates, 0.79 on arithmetic, 0.78 on multiple choice, 0.77 on idiom meanings, 0.72 on \emph{who} questions, and 0.69 on the residual \emph{other} category, which dominates by count ($n=166$) and is where closed-book world knowledge matters most. \section{Analysis and Limitations} The distillation transfers the frontier layer's judgment patterns but also its knowledge gaps: closed-book Bangladesh-specific facts that the teacher verified via live web search are now answered from the student's parametric knowledge alone. The deterministic arithmetic layer is immune to fold shift only insofar as the template families recur; unparsed math rows fall back to the judge, which learned a strong hallucinated prior for closed-book math. Label noise in the pseudo-labels bounds the student: we mitigated with cross-judge consistency filtering and exact verification where possible, and we quantify teacher quality at 0.95 accuracy on the 41 closed-book rows with derivable ground truth. Finally, thresholds are calibrated on 299 rows; we deliberately chose flat-region medians over argmax values to reduce variance. \section{Compliance and Reproducibility} All inference-time models are open-weight (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct base + our LoRA adapter; both attached as Kaggle datasets/models), no internet access is required, and total weights are $\approx$16\,GB.
